prediction: The report discusses the Fire Management Assistance Grants (FMAGs) under Section 420 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. FMAGs provide federal assistance for fire suppression activities on public or private forest land or grassland that may become a major disaster. The grants require a cost-sharing component with state, local, and tribal governments. FMAGs can be requested when a fire is determined to be out of control and may become a major disaster. Under the Sandy Recovery Improvements Act of 2013, tribes have the same authority as states to request FMAG declarations. Assistance provided under FMAGs includes equipment, personnel, and other resources for fire suppression activities. The report answers frequently asked questions about how FMAGs are requested, the types of assistance provided, and cost-sharing requirements. Some tribal lands are managed by the federal government and receive fire suppression support from the National Interagency Fire Center, while others may be eligible for FMAGs. FMAGs cannot be used in conjunction with emergency suppression assistance from federal agencies, but may be used for suppression operations on nonfederal lands under certain circumstances. The report also clarifies that most fires that begin on federal land are the responsibility of the federal agency and are not eligible for FMAG assistance, but exceptions may apply for fires on lands with a mix of federal and nonfederal ownership.

answers: Section 420 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (P.L. 93-288, hereinafter the Stafford Act) authorizes the President to "declare" a Fire Management Assistance Grant (FMAG). In the interest of saving time, the authority to make the declaration has been delegated to the Federal Emergency Management Agency's (FEMA's) Regional Administrators. Once issued, the FMAG declaration authorizes various forms of federal fire suppression assistance such as the provision of equipment, personnel, and grants to state, local, and tribal governments for the control, management, and mitigation of any fire on certain public or private forest land or grassland that might become a major disaster. This federal assistance requires a cost-sharing component such that state, local, and tribal governments are responsible for 25% of the expenses. This report answers frequently asked questions about FMAGs. This report will be updated as events warrant.
